iOS Privacy Manifest Checker

Scans your Swift/Objective-C source for Apple's Required Reason API usage (file timestamps, disk space, system boot time, active keyboards, UserDefaults) and checks it against your PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest -- the two most common causes of an App Store Connect rejection with code ITMS-91061 (missing declaration) or ITMS-91055 (invalid reason code). Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node check.mjs .).

More: what is ITMS-91061 and how do I fix it?


Open your project folder in Finder/Explorer, select every .swift/.m/.mm/.h file plus PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy (select-all works), then choose them here. Not at your project right now? instead.

No files selected yet.

Common questions

Why did App Store Connect reject my app with ITMS-91061 (Missing privacy manifest)?

Your app (or an SDK it embeds) calls one of Apple's Required Reason APIs -- file timestamps, disk space, system boot time, active keyboards, or UserDefaults -- without a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file declaring an approved reason. This tool scans your source for those calls and tells you exactly which category and file is missing a declaration.

What does ITMS-91055 (Invalid API reason declaration) mean?

Your manifest declares a reason code that Apple doesn't recognise for that category -- often a code copy-pasted from a different category's example. This tool checks every declared code against Apple's published list per category and flags any that don't match.

Is my source code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Does a clean report mean Apple will approve my app?

No. This is evidence of what your code and your manifest currently say, produced by pattern-matching known API symbols -- it is not App Review, and it cannot see reflection, dynamic dispatch, or third-party SDK binaries. Always confirm against Apple's current documentation before submitting.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the files you selected and what your manifest declares. It cannot see reflection, dynamically loaded code, or the internals of third-party SDK binaries, and Apple can add categories or reason codes at any time. A clean report is not a guarantee App Review will pass -- verify against Apple's current documentation before you submit, and pick the reason code that actually matches why your code uses the API.

Preparing the store listing for the same release? App Store Screenshot & Icon Checker reads your listing images' own header bytes and flags what the upload will refuse -- an app icon declaring an alpha channel, a HEIC wearing a .png extension, a screenshot set whose members disagree about their size. The other half of "catch it before the store does", at the same point in the release as this tool.

WordPress Plugin Review Checker cross-checks a readme.txt Stable tag against the plugin header's Version, plus unescaped output and missing nonce checks -- the same "read a manifest you already have, name the exact mismatch" shape as this tool, for wordpress.org Plugin Review.

missing-privacy-manifest-itms-91061.html.text:
Fixing ITMS-91061 and ITMS-91055

ITMS-91061: "Missing privacy manifest"

App Store Connect returns this when your app -- or an SDK it embeds -- calls one of Apple's five Required Reason API categories and no PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file in the app bundle declares an approved reason for it. It doesn't matter whether the call is deliberate or came in through a dependency; Apple checks the compiled binary's symbol table, not your intent.

ITMS-91055: "Invalid API reason declaration"

You have a manifest, but one of its declared reason codes isn't on Apple's published list for that category. The most common cause is copy-pasting an entry from one category's example while changing only the NSPrivacyAccessedAPIType string -- the reason codes are not interchangeable between categories.

The five Required Reason API categories

CategoryTypical trigger
File timestampcreationDate, modificationDate, stat()/fstat()/lstat(), getattrlist()
System boot timeProcessInfo.processInfo.systemUptime, mach_absolute_time()
Disk spacevolumeAvailableCapacityKey, systemFreeSize, statfs()
Active keyboardUITextInputMode.activeInputModes
User defaultsUserDefaults, NSUserDefaults, SwiftUI's @AppStorage

Find the exact file and line

The checker on this site scans your source for these symbols, reads your manifest, and tells you exactly which category is used-but-undeclared or declared-with-an-invalid-code, with the file and line for every match. It runs as a browser tool (nothing uploaded) or a Node CLI you can add to your own pre-submission check.

This is evidence of what the code and the manifest say, not a determination that App Review will pass -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it can and can't see, and verify against Apple's current documentation before you resubmit.

vs-waiting-for-app-review.html.text:
← iOS Privacy Manifest Checker

This checker vs. guessing from Apple's docs or waiting for App Review to reject the build

Apple's documentation names the five Required Reason API categories and the reason codes it publishes for each -- it is the source of truth this tool's own category and code list is checked against. What it does not do is read your specific source files or your specific PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy and tell you which category you actually triggered, in which file, or whether the code you declared is even valid for that category. That cross-check has always meant either a guess informed by the docs, or a definite answer from an ITMS-91061/ITMS-91055 rejection days later.

What each approach actually gives you

Apple's documentation is complete and authoritative about what the categories and codes are. It is not a scanner: it cannot look at your project and tell you that DiskSpaceChecker.swift line 6 calls systemFreeSize with no matching manifest entry, because it has never seen your code.

App Review will eventually tell you, with certainty -- after a submission, a review cycle, and a rejection naming the exact code. For a Required Reason API call buried inside a third-party SDK's compiled binary rather than your own source, that rejection may be the first time anyone on the team learns the dependency uses one at all.

This checker runs the same category-and-code cross-check App Review runs, against your source and manifest, before you submit -- in the browser (nothing uploaded) or as a Node CLI you can gate CI on.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which category does my code trigger, and where?This checker's scan -- file and line, free, nothing uploaded.
What are the valid reason codes for a category?This checker lists them per category; both it and Apple's docs agree, since this tool's list is checked against Apple's published one.
Will App Review actually approve my build?Neither. Only Apple's own review determines that -- this is evidence about your source and manifest as they stand today.
Is my source code uploaded anywhere?No. The browser tool reads files with the File API; the CLI never makes a network call.

Common questions

Doesn't Apple's own documentation already explain this?

It lists the five Required Reason API categories and the published reason codes for each, and it is the source of truth this tool's own category and code list is checked against. What it doesn't do is read your specific source files or your specific PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy and tell you which category you actually triggered, in which file, on which line, or whether the code you declared is even one of the valid ones for that category. That cross-check is what used to mean either guessing from the docs or finding out from a rejection.

What does waiting for App Review actually cost?

A submission-review-rejection cycle, at minimum -- often a day or more before ITMS-91061 or ITMS-91055 comes back, and then the same wait again after the fix. For a category buried in a third-party SDK's compiled binary rather than your own code, the first rejection may be the only way you learn the SDK uses a Required Reason API at all. Scanning your source and manifest before you submit catches the same defect without spending a review cycle to find it.

Can I just search my code by hand for these API calls?

You can, and for a small project it may be faster than downloading a tool. The risk is coverage: five categories, each with several trigger symbols (stat(), systemUptime, UserDefaults, and more), across every .swift, .m, .mm, and .h file in the project plus whatever a dependency's own compiled binary calls -- Apple's own review checks the compiled symbol table, not just the files you remembered to grep. This tool runs the same symbol list against every file you point it at, in the browser or as a CI-gating CLI, so a category buried in a file you didn't think to check is not the one that reaches App Review first.

Does a clean report from this tool replace App Review?

No, and it is not built to. This is pattern-matching against known API symbol names in the source and manifest you point it at -- it cannot see reflection, dynamically loaded code, or the internals of a third-party SDK's compiled binary, and Apple can add categories or reason codes at any time. A clean report means your current source and manifest agree with each other and with Apple's published list; it is not a guarantee App Review will pass, so verify against Apple's current documentation before you submit.
